title: Why Southeast Asia Bans Durian on Subways & Why Mixing It With Rum Blocks Liver Enzymes — Subway Bans & Library Gas-Leak Evacuations, Li, Schieberle & Steinhaus's 2-Compound Durian Simulation (Ethyl (2S)-2-Methylbutanoate + 1-pg/L 1-(Ethylsulfanyl)ethane-1-thiol), Teh's 4-Copy Durian MGL Genome Expansion (PDB 1GC0, 2RFV) & Plant L-Ethionine, and Maninang's ~70% Diethyl Disulfide Thiol–Disulfide Inactivation of Cys302–Cys301/303 Inside Human Mitochondrial ALDH2 (PDB 1O01, 3N80)

teenKit.tldr: Southeast Asia bans the spiky durian fruit on subways and hotels because just two hyper-potent chemical compounds can mimic a toxic gas leak, even triggering university library evacuations. When mixed with alcohol like rum, these sulfur compounds block a critical liver enzyme, shutting down your body's ability to process toxins.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding how a simple fruit weaponizes chemistry gives us a masterclass in predictive toxicology, showing how microscopic molecules can literally hijack human organs and spark municipal hazmat responses.
keyTakeaways: Out of dozens of scent chemicals in a durian, just two specific compounds—an ester and a sulfur-heavy thiol—recreate its entire infamous smell.
A rare genetic duplication in the durian's evolutionary history lets it pump out unusual 2-carbon sulfur compounds that standard plant enzymes can't normally make.
Consuming durian with alcohol blocks human mitochondrial ALDH2 by roughly 70%, trapping toxic byproducts inside your liver cells.

vocab.meaning: Tiny molecules that easily evaporate into the air at room temperature, floating straight into your nose to create smells.
An organic sulfur compound known for intensely foul, skunk-like, or rotting odors, even at unimaginably small concentrations.
A plant enzyme that breaks down amino acids to help generate the sulfur compounds responsible for the durian's punch.
A crucial human mitochondrial enzyme responsible for breaking down toxic cellular byproducts and alcohol.

quiz.question: Why does the durian fruit frequently cause public panic and building evacuations, like the one at RMIT University?
options: It contains high-pressure gas pockets that explode when dropped.
It releases ultra-potent sulfur thiols that mimic a dangerous chemical gas leak.
It carries a highly contagious and toxic mold spore on its spikes.
It naturally produces carbon monoxide gas in enclosed spaces.
quiz.explanation: Trace amounts of thiols in the air are so intensely pungent that human noses and detectors register them as hazardous gas leaks.

quiz.question: What role does genetic mutation play in making the durian so uniquely smelly?
options: A paleopolyploid 4-copy gene expansion supercharges its ability to produce specialized sulfur compounds.
It mutated to completely lose all genes responsible for making pleasant sweet sugars.
It evolved a bacterial symbiosis that rots the fruit from the inside out.
It replicates human sweat gland DNA to attract mammals.
quiz.explanation: The durian's genome expanded through ancient whole-genome duplications, creating multiple active copies of the MGL enzyme that pump out heavy sulfur aromas.

quiz.question: Why is mixing durian with alcohol historically warned against in traditional folklore and confirmed by modern science?
options: It instantly turns the stomach contents into a fizzy, explosive foam.
It permanently blinds the person consuming them due to methanol production.
It blocks mitochondrial ALDH2 enzymes, preventing the body from clearing toxins effectively.
It causes an immediate, fatal drop in core body temperature.
quiz.explanation: Compounds like diethyl disulfide in durian inhibit liver ALDH2 by about 70%, impairing toxin clearance and causing severe physical distress.
